Assessing Information in Asynchronous Communication†

By KYLE SCHIRMANN, PRITHWIRAJ (RAJ) CHOUDHURY, MIGUEL ESPINOSA, TARUN KHANNA, AND CHRISTOS A. MAKRIDIS*

Organizations are often viewed as information processors (Galbraith, 1974; Tushman and Nadler, 1978). An efficient, robust information architecture can be a source of competitive advantage (Argote and Ingram, 2000), and intraorganizational flows can be economically salient (Aral, Brynjolfsson and Van Alstyne, 2007). However, measuring the content and flow of information is challenging. In the vein of recent work examining asynchronous communication within firms (Yang et al., 2022; Zuzul et al., 2025), we implement three metrics for capturing aspects of these products and processes from text data, including a metric that considers how unique information is to its audiences. We also leverage a field experiment to determine how the structure of work—specifically, hybrid work arrangements—affects these metrics, finding that workers who split their time between home and the office may be particularly effective at transmitting useful information.

## I. Background

In 2020, we conducted a field experiment in collaboration with a large, Dhaka-based nongovernmental organization. Our experiment concerns 130 workers in the corporate HR function at the headquarter office. Prior to the global pandemic, these workers had spent all five days in the office, and all were shocked into an exclusively work-from-home (WFH) modality in March 2020. As conditions in Bangladesh changed, the organization began transitioning workers back to the office in July 2020. However, given health, safety, and social distancing considerations, the office could only accomodate a limited number of workers on any given day. Given the capacity constraints (generally around 35%), we conducted a daily lottery to determine which workers would be assigned to work from home or from the office on a given day. Workers were told that higher management would be distributing a weekly schedule of office attendance during the prior weekend. The experiment ran for a total of nine weeks, from July 5 to September 3, 2020. A random number generator selected which workers should come to the office each day, and each worker received their schedule for the following week each weekend. At the end of the experiment, all subjects were asked to complete a demographic survey. After workers had completed their surveys (i.e., in the tenth week), they were informed of the experiment and were asked to give their consent for sharing their email data to be used for research purposes. The IT department supplied complete copies of the email mailboxes for the 106 consenting workers, including subjects, message bodies, attachments, and complete to/CC/BCC information. At the conclusion of the experiment, workers were categorized into three groups based on how many days they were exogenously assigned to work from home: high WFH (on average, more than 3 days per week spent working from home), intermediate WFH (2-3), and low WFH (fewer than 2). The balance of the days were worked from the office. Further details of the experiment may be found in Choudhury et al. (2024).

## II. Data and Measurement

The complete email corpus consists of 32,745 emails sent between 106 workers who consented to sharing, of which 53% were sent during the pre-experimental period and the balance during the experiment.1 The corpus also contains 30,323 attachments, also 53% pre-experimental, which consisted primarily of PDFs, spreadsheets, text documents, and images. The body of each email was preprocessed to remove email signatures, inline replies, and the like. Plaintext was recovered from 83% of email attachments. The 3% of documents not in English were machine translated. Each document (email text or attachment text) was then converted into a 200-element vector representation with Doc2vec (Le and Mikolov, 2014). This process is similar to principal component analysis; beyond a mere bag-of-words approach, this method attempts to leverage semantic relationships, considering context to determine the key components of each document. Next, we considered three different metrics to capture different aspects of information generation and circulation within the organization.

A. Production: Information Novelty

We first consider the range of information produced or relayed by a given individual by determining how novel the messages they send are (i.e., how distinctive they are relative to the individual’s other messages). This concept makes no reference to the novelty perceived by the recipients of these messages. Given the document vectors, we apply a clustering algorithm (Zhang, Ramakrishnan and Livny, 1997) to group these vectors into different clusters. For example, one cluster might retrospectively represent “payroll reports,” although the process is unsupervised and the labels are not predetermined. Next, we calculate the cosine similarity between each document and a synthetic centroid document within each cluster; thus, a document’s novelty is defined in reference to its type. We transform this into a novelty measure by taking the additive inverse and linearly mapping the range to [0, 1]. Thus, a high value on this metric indicates that a document is more novel relative to others of the same type. Finally, we take the difference between the average novelty of a sender’s documents within the experimental period and within the pre-experimental period and standardize the variable.

B. Consumption: Information Uniqueness

While novelty can shed light on the diversity of information produced or relayed by a worker, it makes no reference to how a recipient might value it. To consider the value of information in consumption, we turn to another conceptualization of the value of information: “information uniqueness.” While calculated at the level of a sender, this metric inherently centers audience evaluations of information. To do so, we adapt the information uniqueness measure of Aral and Dhillon (2023) to focus primarily on individual senders, rather than dyadic interactions per se. This first stage of the adaptation is nearly identical to their method, except for the specific norm. We consider all intraorganizational sender s ∈S and recipient r dyads. The average vector representation of all documents sent in each directed dyad ⟨s,r⟩is computed as msr. We also calculate mS\r, the average vector representation of documents sent to r by every sender excluding s. We then compute the information uniqueness implied by this dyad as

C. Novel Email Attachments

As a third gloss, we apply a cruder measure: the count of novel email attachments sent by workers. We first calculate the MD5 hash (Rivest, 1992) of each attachment, including images from which text was not extracted. This hash—which considers only the content of an attachment, not its filename or metadata—allows us to determine if attachments differ. Even if two attachments’ content differ by a single bit, their respective hashes will be distinct. Then, for each attachment, we determine if it is the first time that its content has ever been sent within the organization. The novel attachment count is then accrued to its first sender, again within the experimental and pre-experimental periods. Note that we do not claim that novel attachments have any relationship to productivity or creativity: some workers, for example, may routinely generate periodic reporting spreadsheets or process standard forms. However, this metric does complement the two metrics previously mentioned.

## III. Results

*Table 1 reports the results of these three metrics for information content and flows. We find support for the intermediate WFH condition inducing higher increases in information novelty and uniqueness, both in the unsaturated (column 1) and saturated (column 2) specifications. We also find suport for the intermediate WFH condition inducing a higher increase in the count of novel email attachments, but only in the saturated specification. Thus, employees and managers in the intermediate WFH condition, relative to the low or high WFH conditions, appear to relay more novel information and information that is more distinctive to its recipients. Note that the coefficient on the low WFH condition is not significant at the p < 0.10 level in any specification. We also find that non-manager report*

This is consistent with a view of managers as engaging in more cognitively demanding tasks, and these results also suggest that the information metrics are not being driven by routine reporting (usually generated by non-managers for consumption by a manager). Note that we do not consider temporality in our information metrics, with the exception of the MD5-based measure which, by construction, generates a one-time signal. Further work might specifically model these dynamics, paying particular attention to novel ideas that resonate in later time periods (Barron et al., 2018). We also considered similar metrics, such as “usefulness,” in determining what these metrics are meant to capture. An HR manager manually reviewed a sample of 100 emails, one drawn from each percentile of the information novelty distribution, and scored them for usefulness (as the manager interpreted the term) on a scale from 1–5. We then applied a supervised learning process to predict the expected usefulness score for each out-of-sample document. Specifically, we trained a support vector machine classifier, using a sigmoid kernel, with the Doc2vec representations as the feature set and the manually-scored usefulness as the label. Next, we predicted the usefulness scores of all documents. The correlation between the information novelty metric and the manager’s usefulness score was 0.26. Owing to the small sample size and single scorer, caution should be employed in interpreting this correlation. However, the positive correlation between usefulness and information uniqueness is consistent with an interpretation of information novelty being a desirable trait in determining usefulness.2

## IV. Conclusion

Using three metrics of information, the experiment examined the content of information flows and how well they matched their audiences. With the exception of the last metric on pure novelty— which was measured by a count of distinctive attachments relayed by workers—the results suggest that hybrid work may cause workers to transmit more diverse information and also information that is distinctive to its recipients. The novelty metric was also shown to be correlated positively with a manager-judged “usefulness” score, suggesting that this result is of managerial importance. In effect, workers in the intermediate WFH position functioned as brokers, collecting and generating novel communications and connecting groups with diverse knowledge bases.3 This experiment concluded in 2020, and its genesis was the result of external circumstance (because, given the pandemic, the organization’s hand was forced) and a deliberate choice (the hunch that hybrid work might be worth a shot). Hybrid work in this experiment was adopted primarily due to happenstance, not pursued as a deliberate policy; any positive outcomes were serendipitous. Managers, in the future, might introduce a hybrid work structure that maximizes the knowledge available to network members and allows it to flow via individuals who are adept at navigating both in-person and at-home work. In each case, these are deliberate organizational design choices that induce shifts in the information architecture of the firm.
